title: Choosing the Right Model
description: Train three different surrogates on the same 3-input nonlinear dataset and compare their cross-validation scores. You will see why model choice matters and when GPR outperforms Random Forest and Linear models.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 3 inputs (x1, x2, x3) and 1 output (y). Notice the input ranges: x1 and x2 span roughly −π to +π, x3 spans 0 to 5.
Open the scatter matrix. Look at the x1 vs y plot — you should see a sinusoidal pattern. Look at x3 vs y — that should look more linear.

quiz.question: Given a mix of nonlinear (sinusoidal) and linear relationships in the same dataset, which model type would you expect to struggle most?
quiz.explanation: A linear model assumes all inputs relate to the output through a straight line. It cannot capture the sin(x1)·cos(x2) term here without feature engineering. GPR and RF can fit nonlinear patterns directly.

steps.instruction: Designate x1, x2, x3 as inputs and y as the output.
Apply Min-Max normalization to all three inputs.
First run: configure as Linear model, test split 0.2, 5-fold CV. Train and note the R² score.

quiz.question: Cross-validation R² measures model fit on the training data (k-fold held-out folds). Why is CV R² more informative than the training R²?
options: Training R² is always 1.0 so it is useless
CV R² estimates how well the model generalises to unseen data, not just how well it memorised the training set
CV R² uses more data points
quiz.explanation: A model can achieve R²=1.0 on training data simply by memorising every point (overfitting). CV holds out a different fold each iteration and measures accuracy on data the model never saw — a much better proxy for real-world performance.

steps.instruction: Note the test R² for Linear. Now go back to Configure, switch to GPR, and retrain. Then try Random Forest. Which model achieves the highest test R²?

quiz.question: For this 150-row, 3-input, nonlinear dataset, what is the most likely ranking of models by test R²?
quiz.explanation: GPR and RF both capture nonlinearity. GPR typically wins on smooth, small datasets where its kernel perfectly models correlation structure. RF wins on noisy, high-dimensional, or irregular data. Both soundly outperform Linear on sinusoidal responses.

steps.instruction: Use the best-performing model to predict y at x1=0, x2=0, x3=2.5. The true value is sin(0)·cos(0) + 0.3×2.5 = 0.75.
